served.stem: 3-Phenyl-1,5-hexadiene (drawn) is heated, allowing a Cope ([3,3]-sigmatropic) rearrangement to reach the more stable isomer. Which structure is that product?
served.bankWhy: The Cope [3,3] shift of the 1,5-diene breaks the C3-C4 sigma bond and forms a new C1-C6 bond, relocating the double bonds. The phenyl ends up conjugated with a newly formed alkene (styrene-type), giving 1-phenylhexa-1,5-diene (opt 0), which is thermodynamically favored. Option 1 is the unchanged starting material; the others have incorrect connectivity or form a ring.

answer.line: The Cope breaks C3-C4, joins C1 to C6 and moves both pi bonds. The new C=C lands beside the ring, so that side wins.

steps: Mark the six carbons: C1=C2, C3 holding the phenyl, C4, then C5=C6.
Move three pairs at once. The C3-C4 sigma bond breaks, a new C1-C6 bond forms, and the pi bonds shift to C2=C3 and C4=C5.
The reaction runs both ways, so it settles on the more stable side. Now C2=C3 sits on the phenyl carbon, conjugated with the ring: 1-phenylhexa-1,5-diene.

choices.note: This is the starting diene, drawn turned around: the same molecule. No bond has moved yet.

choices.display: a vinyl and a butenyl group on neighboring ring carbons
choices.note: A group landing on the ortho ring carbon is the aromatic Claisen pattern, from allyl aryl ethers. A Cope never touches the ring.
One sigma bond out, one in, both pi bonds moved, and the new C=C conjugated with the ring.
One pi bond moved, but the sigma bond never broke and the other pi bond stayed put. A [3,3] shift moves all three pairs.
The six-membered ring belongs to the chair-shaped transition state and to Diels-Alder products. The Cope product is still an open chain, and this choice has lost two H.
